stories.title: Trace state versions to find overwritten agent work
stories.summary: A tracing guide shows how to record state versions and commit outcomes to reveal concurrent agent runs that overwrite one another.
body: Telemetry.dev is an AI observability service that traces model calls, tools and retrievals. Its guide addresses a less visible failure in stateful agents: two runs can read the same checkpoint, then the later write can overwrite the first run's work. Individual operations may all appear successful, so ordinary latency and error signals need not reveal the lost update.

The guide recommends recording a state version when the application loads it, on a span, a record of one operation within a trace. At commit time, the application records the expected version, current version and outcome. A conditional write rejects a commit if the stored version has changed. Engineers can then compare the two spans and search for another run on the same thread that committed between them. The example attribute names are application-defined, not automatic OpenTelemetry conventions.

The author describes serializing runs per thread or reloading and reconciling conflicting changes as possible responses. The instrumentation only detects paths that emit it, requires a usable version marker, and cannot establish whether the state itself is correct. A blind overwrite can still succeed even if recorded versions expose the mismatch.
stories.takeaway: Engineers running concurrent stateful agents can instrument a critical read and commit path, then check whether their store actually rejects stale writes.
stories.score_reason: A concrete, source-supported tracing method for diagnosing lost updates in stateful agents, with explicit limitations.

source_evidence.method: Original article time element and article:published_time agree with the visible publisher date.

stories.title: Phoenix prevents cancelled loader batches from freezing its server
stories.summary: A Phoenix server release changes how cancelled data-loader batches are checked, addressing a freeze that can affect trace pages and health checks.
body: Arize Phoenix is an open-source platform for tracing and evaluating AI applications. Its server release fixes a cancellation problem that could make the server stop responding while users inspect large traces. According to the change's maintainer, a failed field or a cancelled request could leave pages, API calls and health checks waiting while the server processed a large batch of pending lookups.

The pull request explains the cause: as each lookup was cancelled, the underlying loader checked the whole batch again. The fix substitutes a batch implementation that resumes its checks where the previous check stopped, so each lookup is checked approximately once. Phoenix installs the change when the application starts. Tests compare its database-read cancellation behavior with the original loader and check the work involved in large cancellations.

The maintainer reports shorter health-check waits in direct tests, while noting that the freeze did not reproduce in a small browser trial. The change does not fix time spent building an ordinary large trace response or a separate upstream defect where cancellation can reach other callers sharing a cached key. A version guard in the tests prompts maintainers to reassess the patch when the underlying loader changes.
stories.takeaway: Teams operating Phoenix with large traces should review the server release and check responsiveness during failed or cancelled trace loads.
stories.score_reason: A server reliability fix directly affects access to AI traces, with measured behavior and clearly stated limits.

source_evidence.method: GitHub release API published_at for the stable, non-draft release; linked pull request documents mechanism and tests.
